questions.q: The embryonic liver bud first begins to develop on which day of gestation, and from which division of the primitive gut tube does it arise?
options: 8th day of gestation; Midgut
8th day of gestation; Foregut
25th day of gestation; Foregut
25th day of gestation; Hindgut
questions.explanation: The liver begins developing on the 8th day of gestation as a bud from the foregut, and it becomes clearly visible by the 25th day.

questions.q: During hepatic development, the embryonic liver bud splits into cranial and caudal divisions. Which of the following correctly describes the fate of the cranial part (pars hepatica)?
options: It forms the gallbladder and cystic duct.
It forms the hepatic stroma and capsule.
It forms the hepatic parenchyma (hepatocytes and intrahepatic ductal cells).
It forms the Kupffer cells.
questions.explanation: The cranial part (pars hepatica) of the liver bud forms the hepatic parenchyma (hepatocytes and intrahepatic ductal cells), while the caudal part (pars cystica) forms the cystic duct and gallbladder.

questions.q: A medical student is asked to identify the embryological origin of the hepatic capsule and Kupffer cells. Which of the following is the correct source?
options: Endoderm of the foregut
Mesoderm of the septum transversum
Endothelium of the vitelline veins
Ectoderm of the proctodeum
questions.explanation: The hepatic bud invades the surrounding mesoderm of the septum transversum, which gives rise to both the hepatic capsule and the Kupffer cells.

questions.q: The hepatic sinusoids—which sit between columns of hepatocytes—develop from which of the following embryonic structures?
options: The dorsal mesogastrium
The vitelline and umbilical veins
The umbilical artery
The pars cystica
questions.explanation: The liver endothelium is derived from the vitelline and umbilical veins, which anastomose to form the network of liver sinusoids.

questions.q: Which of the following options correctly represents the physiological transition of the liver's weight relative to total body weight throughout development into adulthood?
options: 60th day: 20% → At Birth: 10% → Adult: 5%
60th day: 10% → At Birth: 5% → Adult: 2.5%
60th day: 5% → At Birth: 2.5% → Adult: 1.5%
60th day: 15% → At Birth: 8% → Adult: 3%
questions.explanation: The liver's relative weight ratio shifts from 10% of body weight on the 60th day of gestation, to 5% at birth, and ultimately to 2.5% in adults.

questions.q: What is the average weight of the adult human liver, and how does it rank in size among the body's organs?
options: 500–800 grams; It is the largest overall organ
1200–1800 grams; It is the second-largest organ overall (after the skin)
1200–1800 grams; It is the third-largest organ overall (after the skin and brain)
2000–2500 grams; It is the largest visceral organ
questions.explanation: The adult liver weighs on average 1200–1800 grams, making it the second-largest organ in the body (after the skin) and the largest visceral organ.

questions.q: Anatomical lobes of the liver are divided into a small left lobe and a very large right lobe. What peritoneal and ligamentous structures mark this division on the superior/anterior and inferior surfaces?
options: Cantlie's line superiorly; Gallbladder fossa inferiorly
Falciform ligament superiorly/anteriorly; Round ligament (ligamentum teres) inferiorly
Coronary ligament superiorly; Ligamentum venosum inferiorly
Gastrocolic omentum superiorly; Lesser omentum inferiorly
questions.explanation: The division between the anatomical lobes is defined by the falciform ligament on the superior and anterior surfaces, and the round ligament (ligamentum teres) on the inferior surface.

questions.q: A surgeon planning a formal right hemihepatectomy uses "Cantlie's Line" to divide the liver into equal surgical (physiological) lobes. What are the correct surface landmarks for Cantlie's Line?
options: From the falciform ligament to the ligamentum venosum
From the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) posteriorly
From the caudate lobe to the quadrate lobe
From the right triangular ligament to the porta hepatis
questions.explanation: Physiological (surgical) lobes are split into equal halves by Cantlie's Line, which runs from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the IVC posteriorly.

questions.q: Which of the following options correctly describes the division of the surgical sectors (sections) of the left and right lobes of the liver?
options: Left lobe is divided by coronal plane; Right lobe is divided by falciform ligament
Left lobe is divided into anterior/posterior sectors; Right lobe is divided into lateral/medial sectors
Left lobe is divided by the falciform ligament into lateral and medial sectors; Right lobe is divided by a coronal plane into anterior and posterior sectors
Both lobes are divided into superior and inferior sectors by a horizontal transverse plane
questions.explanation: The left lobe is divided by the falciform ligament into lateral and medial sectors, whereas the right lobe is divided by a coronal plane into anterior and posterior sectors.

questions.q: How many functional liver segments are recognized transversely based on the distribution of the hepatic veins and portal tracts?
options: 4 segments
5 segments
8 segments
9 segments
questions.explanation: The four sectors of the liver are subdivided transversely into 8 functional segments depending on the branches of the hepatic veins and portal tract distributions.

questions.q: A radiology resident is reviewing an abdominal CT scan. She is asked to locate the "Caudate Lobe." Where is it situated, and what are its boundaries?
options: On the inferior surface, between the gallbladder and the ligamentum teres fissure
On the posterior surface, between the IVC and the fissure for ligamentum venosum
On the superior surface, to the left of the falciform ligament
On the visceral surface, directly adjacent to the renal impression
questions.explanation: The Caudate Lobe lies on the posterior surface of the liver, bounded between the IVC and the fissure for ligamentum venosum.

questions.q: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon identifies the "Quadrate Lobe" next to the gallbladder. What is the correct anatomical position and boundaries of this lobe?
options: On the posterior surface, between the bare area and the IVC
On the superior surface, immediately below the diaphragm
On the inferior (visceral) surface, between the gallbladder and the fissure for ligamentum teres
On the visceral surface, between the renal and colic impressions
questions.explanation: The Quadrate Lobe lies on the inferior (visceral) surface, situated between the gallbladder and the fissure for ligamentum teres.

questions.q: Although the liver is almost completely covered with visceral peritoneum, there are several "bare areas" devoid of peritoneal covering. Which of the following is NOT one of these bare areas?
options: The bare area on the posterior surface (to the right of the IVC)
The gallbladder fossa
The porta hepatis
The gastric impression on the left lobe
questions.explanation: The gastric impression is fully covered in peritoneum. The five bare areas are: (1) the posterior bare area to the right of the IVC, (2) the gallbladder fossa, (3) the groove for the IVC, (4) the porta hepatis, and (5) the bases of the peritoneal ligaments.

questions.q: The lesser omentum is a peritoneal fold connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach to the visceral surface of the liver. Which structures run within its free border, and what opening's anterior boundary do they form?
options: Portal triad; Foramen of Winslow (Epiploic Foramen)
Hepatic veins; Foramen of Winslow
Short gastric vessels; Lesser sac
Gastroduodenal artery; Splenic hilum
questions.explanation: The free border of the lesser omentum contains the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, common bile duct) and forms the anterior boundary of the Foramen of Winslow (Epiploic Foramen).

questions.q: A surgical resident is asked to identify the anatomical boundaries of the Foramen of Winslow (Winslow's Foramen) during a laparotomy. Which of the following pairs is correct?
options: Upper: 1st part of duodenum; Lower: Caudate lobe of liver
Anterior: Portal triad in lesser omentum free border; Posterior: Inferior Vena Cava (IVC)
Anterior: IVC; Posterior: Aorta
Upper: Left kidney; Lower: Transverse colon
questions.explanation: The boundaries of the Foramen of Winslow are: Upper (Caudate lobe of liver), Lower (1st part of duodenum), Anterior (Free border of lesser omentum containing the portal triad), and Posterior (IVC).

questions.q: The liver has a massive, highly unique dual blood supply with a total inflow of approximately 1.5 L/min. Which of the following options correctly represents the flow and oxygen contributions of the portal vein and hepatic artery?
options: Portal Vein: 20% flow, 50% O₂ needs; Hepatic Artery: 80% flow, 50% O₂ needs
Portal Vein: 50% flow, 80% O₂ needs; Hepatic Artery: 50% flow, 20% O₂ needs
Portal Vein: 80% flow, 50% O₂ needs; Hepatic Artery: 20% flow, 50% O₂ needs
Portal Vein: 80% flow, 80% O₂ needs; Hepatic Artery: 20% flow, 20% O₂ needs
questions.explanation: The Portal Vein carries venous blood from the GIT, supplying 80% of the total blood flow and 50% of the liver's oxygen requirements. The Hepatic Artery supplies 20% of the blood flow and 50% of the oxygen requirements.

questions.q: Within the hilum of the liver (porta hepatis), three major structures are arranged in a strict posterior-to-anterior relationship. From posterior to anterior, what is this arrangement?
options: Portal Vein (most posterior) → Hepatic Artery (intermediate) → Right & Left Hepatic Ducts (most anterior)
Hepatic Ducts (most posterior) → Hepatic Artery (intermediate) → Portal Vein (most anterior)
Hepatic Artery (most posterior) → Portal Vein (intermediate) → Hepatic Ducts (most anterior)
Portal Vein (most posterior) → Hepatic Ducts (intermediate) → Hepatic Artery (most anterior)
questions.explanation: At the porta hepatis, the arrangement of structures from posterior to anterior is: (1) Portal Vein, (2) Hepatic Artery, and (3) Right and Left Hepatic Ducts.

questions.q: Hepatic venous blood is drained from the parenchyma and returned to the systemic circulation via:
options: The portal vein directly into the splenic vein
Three hepatic veins draining directly into the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC)
Two hepatic veins draining into the renal veins
The cystic vein directly into the Azygos system
questions.explanation: The outflow of the liver is carried by three hepatic veins that drain directly into the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC).

questions.q: Under the microscope, the classic liver lobule is described as a hexagonal-shaped unit. Which structures occupy the center and the periphery of this lobule, respectively?
options: Central vein at the center; Portal tracts (containing triads) at the periphery
Portal tract at the center; Central veins at the periphery
Central vein at the center; Kupffer cells at the periphery
Space of Disse at the center; Bile canaliculi at the periphery
questions.explanation: The classic liver lobule is arranged around a central vein at its center, with portal tracts (containing portal venules, hepatic arterioles, and bile ductules) situated at the periphery of the lobule.

questions.q: During surgical management of a traumatic liver laceration, the surgeon performs "Pringle's maneuver" (inflow-occlusion) to control bleeding. Which ligament is clamped, and which vessels are occluded?
options: Gastrocolic ligament; Splenic artery and vein
Hepatoduodenal ligament (free border of lesser omentum); Portal vein and hepatic artery
Falciform ligament; Hepatic veins
Coronary ligament; Inferior Vena Cava
questions.explanation: Pringle's maneuver consists of clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament (the free border of the lesser omentum), which temporarily occludes the liver's vascular inflow (portal vein and hepatic artery).

questions.q: A patient with severe liver cirrhosis undergoes a workup for portal hypertension. To which systemic venous system does the esophageal branch of the Left Gastric (Coronary) vein anastomose, forming the classic site for esophageal varices?
options: Superior rectal vein
Retroperitoneal veins of Retzius
Esophageal veins from the Azygos and Hemi-azygos veins
Para-umbilical veins
questions.explanation: At the lower end of the esophagus, the portal tributary (esophageal branches of the left gastric/coronary vein and short gastric veins) anastomoses with the systemic tributary (esophageal veins from the azygos and hemi-azygos veins), forming esophageal varices.

questions.q: In portal hypertension, embryonic channels at the umbilicus open up to connect the portal and systemic systems, clinically presenting as "Caput Medusae." What are the portal and systemic vessels involved in this anastomosis?
options: Superior rectal vein anastomosing with inferior rectal vein
Para-umbilical veins (in the ligamentum teres) anastomosing with superior and inferior epigastric veins
Superior mesenteric vein anastomosing with renal veins
Short gastric veins anastomosing with inferior phrenic veins
questions.explanation: Caput Medusae is formed at the umbilicus by the anastomosis of the para-umbilical vein (portal) with the superior and inferior epigastric veins (systemic).
